reasoning: Decomposed into 72 verifiable statement(s). Completeness check passed. Grouped into 7 reasoning segment(s).

statements: The chief complaint is a 6-week history of sharp left-sided chest pain.
The chest pain is pleuritic.
The chest pain is worse with inspiration.
The chest pain is positional.
The chest pain is worse lying down.
The chest pain is accompanied by progressive back pain.
The chest pain is accompanied by constipation.
The chest pain is accompanied by lower-limb weakness and numbness.
The lower-limb weakness and numbness are concerning for spinal cord compression.
The patient’s own major concern appears to be chest pain plus progressive neurologic symptoms from back involvement.
The salient positive findings strongly suggest an underlying thoracic malignancy with metastatic spread.
Chest radiograph shows a left upper-lobe opacity.
Contrast CT confirms a large 75 mm lobulated left upper-lobe mass.
The left upper-lobe mass directly invades the chest wall.
The left upper-lobe mass invades the left third rib.
The left upper-lobe mass invades adjacent muscle.
There is a mild to moderate left pleural effusion.
MRI spine shows widespread skeletal lesions.
MRI spine shows multiple thoracic paraspinal soft-tissue deposits.
One thoracic paraspinal soft-tissue deposit at T4/T5 is causing significant cord compression.
CT shows vertebral bony lesions.
CT shows pelvic bony lesions.
The back pain worsened by walking.
The lower-limb weakness and numbness fit metastatic spinal disease with cord compression.
The pleuritic chest pain is well explained by pleural and chest wall involvement from the lung mass.
The absence of major hematologic abnormalities does not exclude metastatic solid malignancy.
Normal renal function does not exclude metastatic solid malignancy.
Normal calcium does not exclude metastatic solid malignancy.
He has no smoking history.
Lung cancer still occurs in never-smokers.
Lung cancer in never-smokers is particularly adenocarcinoma.
Normal hemoglobin argues against a classic symptomatic multiple myeloma presentation.
Normal calcium argues against a classic symptomatic multiple myeloma presentation.
Normal renal function argues against a classic symptomatic multiple myeloma presentation.
Normal white count and differential make hematologic malignancy less supported.
There is no hepatomegaly on exam.
There are no described infectious symptoms such as fever.
There are no described infectious symptoms such as productive cough.
There are no described infectious symptoms such as weight loss.
The absence of infectious symptoms does not favor infection such as tuberculosis.
The absence of infectious symptoms does not favor empyema-related disease.
Cardiovascular examination is otherwise normal.
Respiratory examination is otherwise normal.
Primary cardiac causes are much less likely in the face of the imaging findings.
Benign pleuritic causes are much less likely in the face of the imaging findings.
Primary lung carcinoma with osseous metastases fits best.
There is a dominant large left upper-lobe mass with chest wall and rib invasion.
There is a pleural effusion.
There are widespread bone lesions causing cord compression.
Multiple myeloma could explain diffuse skeletal lesions and cord compression.
Multiple myeloma is less convincing because there is a clear primary lung mass.
Multiple myeloma is less convincing because the labs do not show anemia.
Multiple myeloma is less convincing because the labs do not show renal impairment.
Multiple myeloma is less convincing because the labs do not show hypercalcemia.
Metastatic disease from another occult primary is possible in principle.
Diffuse bone metastases can arise from several cancers.
The presence of a large invasive lung mass makes the lung the most likely primary rather than an incidental lesion.
Lymphoma is less likely.
Lymphoma can produce masses and bony involvement.
The imaging pattern of a large lobulated upper-lobe mass invading chest wall and rib with pleural effusion is more typical of primary bronchogenic carcinoma.

The unifying diagnosis that best explains the pleuritic chest pain, left upper-lobe opacity, 75 mm invasive lung mass, pleural effusion, rib and chest wall invasion, widespread vertebral and pelvic lesions, paraspinal soft-tissue deposits, and spinal cord compression is metastatic primary lung cancer.
In a never-smoker, adenocarcinoma is a particularly plausible histologic subtype.
Histology is not directly provided.
The single most likely diagnosis is metastatic non-small cell lung cancer presenting with spinal metastases and cord compression.
CT shows a 75 mm lobulated left upper-lobe mass with chest wall and rib invasion and pleural effusion.
MRI and CT show widespread vertebral, pelvic, and paraspinal metastatic lesions causing cord compression.
Chest pain is pleuritic and consistent with pleural and chest wall involvement.
Metastatic primary lung carcinoma, likely non-small cell lung cancer, is the high-probability diagnosis.
Multiple myeloma is a medium-probability diagnosis.
Metastatic malignancy from another occult primary is a low-probability diagnosis.
Lymphoma is a low-probability diagnosis.
The final diagnosis is metastatic non-small cell lung cancer.
